At the gram sabha meeting in their village near Madurai, the panchayat hall was full of older men. Lakshmi, sixteen, stood up with a sheet of paper in her shaking hand.
Her brother Hrithik had helped her practise all week under the neem tree. “Say what's wrong, why it matters, what you want,” he'd said.
She began. “The girls' toilet at our school has been broken for four months.” A few men muttered. She looked at the back wall, as she'd practised, and kept going. “Twelve girls stopped coming to school. I'm asking the panchayat to fix it before the exams.”
The hall went quiet. The sarpanch nodded slowly and asked for a quote from the mason.
Outside, Hrithik slapped her on the back. Her legs were still trembling.

qa.q: How long had the girls' toilet been broken?
qa.a: It had been broken for four months.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel as she stood up to speak?
qa.a: She felt nervous and scared, her hand shaking and her legs trembling.

qa.q: What helped Lakshmi hold the audience's attention?
qa.a: A clear structure of problem, reason and request, and looking at the back wall to stay steady.

qa.q: How might the sarpanch have seen Lakshmi's speech?
qa.a: He probably saw it as clear and serious, which is why he asked for a quote from the mason.

grounding: A sixteen-year-old structures a talk and manages fear to speak at a village meeting.

In a school hall in Kyoto, Hana, fourteen, waited behind the curtain for the speech contest. Her palms were wet. Her talk was about her grandfather's bicycle repair shop.
Her friend Aiko squeezed her arm. “Remember: pick three friendly faces. Left, middle, right. Talk to them, not the crowd.”
Hana walked out. For the first line, her voice wobbled. She found Aiko in the middle, then a kind-looking teacher on the left, then a boy smiling on the right. She talked to them.
She told the story of the old bicycle her grandfather rebuilt for her. People laughed at the part where the bell fell off.
When she finished, the applause was loud. She didn't win, but three people came up to ask about the shop.

qa.a: Her grandfather's bicycle repair shop.

qa.a: She felt nervous, with wet palms.

qa.a: Talking to three friendly faces instead of the whole crowd, and telling a story.

qa.q: How might Aiko feel watching Hana's speech?
qa.a: Aiko probably feels proud and happy that the tip helped.

At the tea stall in their small town near Belgaum, Manjula, fourteen, sat scrolling short videos on her father's phone while he talked to the stall owner.
Her cousin Jasleen, visiting from Pune, watched her swipe. “How long have you been on that?”
“Five minutes?”
Jasleen showed her the screen-time page. Forty-two minutes.
Manjula stared. “It felt like five.”
“It never ends, that's the trick. No bottom of the page. Every swipe is a little surprise, like a lottery.”
“So they want me stuck?”
“They get paid for your time.”
Manjula locked the phone and handed it back to her father. Then she asked Jasleen to teach her the card game she'd seen her play.

I'm Rehana, Eshaan's older sister. Last month, Eshaan, sixteen, posted a meme mocking his maths teacher's accent on his class group. Everyone laughed. He deleted it an hour later when he started to feel bad.
But someone had already taken a screenshot. By the next morning, it was on three other groups, and a parent had forwarded it to the principal.
I watched my brother sit on the stairs with his head in his hands. He said, “I deleted it. Why is it still there?”
He wrote a real apology to the teacher, in person, not online. The teacher accepted it, but said, “Remember, the internet doesn't forget.”
Now Eshaan reads every post twice before sending. Sometimes he doesn't send at all.

qa.a: The teacher was probably hurt and embarrassed by the mockery.

I saw Hafsa type the question into an AI tool. It gave her a smooth paragraph and a list of four books. I thought she'd just copy it.

Then she closed the tool and wrote her own essay from our textbook and one real book from the list. She used the AI only to ask it questions and check if she understood.

The door slammed so hard the pictures rattled.
Pradeep knocked a few minutes later. “Parul? Can I come in?”
“Whatever.”
He sat on the edge of her desk chair. “You want to tell me what happened?”
“Nothing happened. That's the problem. I'm just… angry. At everything. Then I want to cry.”
Pradeep nodded slowly. “At your age, moods can swing fast. Your body's changing a lot.”
“So it's not my fault?”

“The door will live. Want to go get chai?”

In the school counsellor's office, Sangeeta, seventeen, sat beside her mother Ankita. The theatre club's rehearsals ran till eight, and her mother wanted her home by seven.
“Seven is the rule,” Ankita said.
“But I'll miss the last hour, and I'm the lead.”
The counsellor asked each of them what they were worried about.
“Safety,” said her mother. “The road is dark.”
“Letting my team down,” said Sangeeta.
They worked out a deal: rehearsals till eight, but Sangeeta would text when leaving, travel with two friends, and be home by 8:30. If she broke it once, they'd go back to seven.
Ankita sighed, then nodded. Sangeeta squeezed her hand.

qa.a: The theatre club's rehearsals ran till eight.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel about Sangeeta coming home later?
qa.a: She felt worried about safety because the road is dark.

qa.q: What made the negotiation respectful and successful?
qa.a: Each said what worried them, and they made a clear deal with conditions that addressed safety and trust.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel about the deal?
qa.a: She felt grateful and relieved, squeezing her mother's hand.

grounding: A seventeen-year-old and her mother negotiate a curfew respectfully with a counsellor's help.

passage:
Francis, you asked how I got my parents to trust me. Honestly, at fourteen I didn't. I'm Vandana, and back then every argument was about time. When to be home, where I'd been, why my phone was off.
My mother said something once that stuck. “Trust is like savings. You add a little every time.”
So I started small. I told them where I was, even when they didn't ask. I came home ten minutes early. When I was late once, I called before, not after.
After six months, they let me stay out till nine for a friend's birthday. After a year, I could go to the city library alone.
I'm seventeen now. They still worry. But they trust me.

qa.q: What did Vandana's mother compare trust to?
qa.a: Savings.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel about the arguments at fourteen?
qa.a: Vandana felt frustrated and stuck in constant fights about time.

qa.q: What approach helped Vandana earn more freedom?
qa.a: Adding small bits of trust: saying where Vandana was going, coming home early and calling before being late.

qa.q: How might Vandana's parents feel now?
qa.a: They still worry, but feel more at ease trusting Vandana.

grounding: A seventeen-year-old explains how trust was built with parents step by step to gain more independence.

passage:
When the Class 10 results came, I was fourth in my class. I'm Seema. I'd been first for three years.
At dinner, my father Shankar looked at the report card for a long time. Then he said, “What happened?” I went to my room without eating.
That night I lay awake thinking I was a failure. Fourth. As if the number was all of me.
The next morning Papa knocked. He sat on my bed. “I was wrong last night. I asked the wrong question. I should've asked how you are.”
I cried. I told him how tired I'd been, how scared of not being first.
He said, “You're my daughter, not your rank.”
I still want to do well. But I'm learning the number isn't me.

qa.q: What rank did Seema get in Class 10?
qa.a: Fourth.

qa.q: How did Seema feel on the night of the results?
qa.a: She felt worthless and ashamed, like a failure, as if her rank was all of her.

qa.q: What did Shankar do the next morning that helped?
qa.a: He admitted he asked the wrong question, asked how Seema was, and said she was more than her rank.

qa.q: How might Shankar have felt after seeing Seema's reaction?
qa.a: He probably felt regretful and worried, realising his words had hurt her.

grounding: A teenager learns, with her father's apology, that her rank does not define her worth.

Class teacher's note, Class 11. Tanvir Ahmed.
Mridul (sixteen), usually first in class, came ninth in the mid-term exams. This week he stopped eating lunch and sat alone. Today, when I returned his paper, he said quietly, “I'm useless. My parents will be so disappointed.”
I took the words seriously. At break I sat with him in the empty classroom. I told him one exam does not measure his worth, and asked how he was really feeling. He said he couldn't sleep.
The same afternoon I took him to the school counsellor, Ms Mehta, who spoke with him and then called his parents. They came in after school.
Next step: weekly check-ins with Mridul and a class talk on rank pressure.

qa.q: What rank did Mridul get in the mid-term exams?
qa.a: Ninth.

qa.q: How was Mridul feeling after the results?
qa.a: He felt hopeless and worthless, calling himself useless and not sleeping.

qa.q: What did the teacher do right when Mridul said he was useless?
qa.a: He took it seriously, talked with Mridul, took him to the counsellor and involved his parents the same day.

qa.q: How might Mridul's parents feel when they are called to school?
qa.a: They may feel worried but grateful the school noticed, and want to support him.

grounding: A teacher responds the same day to a sixteen-year-old struggling with rank and self-worth.

Sunday night
Family lunch today. Deepika-didi got 98% in the boards and everyone kept saying it. Dadi looked at me and said, “And you, Darshan? You'll do the same next year, na?”
I nodded and ate my rice very slowly.
Later, Deepika found me on the terrace. I thought she'd brag. Instead she said, “Everyone thinks I was calm. I cried every night for two months.”
I didn't know that.
She said, “Don't try to be me. Just do your best and tell someone when it's too much.”
I told her I'm scared of disappointing everyone. She said she was too.
I'm still scared. But now I know I'm not the only one. — Darshan

qa.a: That she had cried every night too, and that Darshan should do their best and tell someone when it's too much.

qa.a: She probably feels close to Darshan and glad she shared her own struggle.
